parts.problem_md: State Hubble's law.
parts.solution_md:
Hubble's law states:

**EITHER**

- The (recessional) speed of a galaxy is (directly) proportional to its distance from the Earth; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- $H_{0}=\frac{v}{d}$, where *v* = speed of recession of galaxy (from observer), *d *= distance of galaxy (away from observer); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

**Extract:**

Hubble's law states: The (recessional) speed of a galaxy is (directly) proportional to its distance from the Earth; OR H_0 = v/d, where v = speed of recession of galaxy (from observer), d = distance of galaxy (away from observer).

Explain how the Hubble constant can be used to determine an age for the universe.
parts.solution_md:
The Hubble constant can be used to determine an age for the universe from:

- $H_{0}=\frac{v}{d}$, the Hubble constant $H_{0}$ has units of s<sup>−1</sup>
- (Therefore) the age of the universe = $\frac{1}{H_{0}}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Notice *$\frac{1}{H_{0}}$* will have units of **s** (seconds) which can then be converted into years for the age of the universe.*

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Explain how the Hubble constant can be used to determine an age for the universe.

The Hubble constant can be used to determine an age for the universe from: H_0 = v/d, the Hubble constant H_0 has units of s^−1. (Therefore) the age of the universe = 1/H_0

The Hubble constant is estimated to be 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the age of the Universe in years.

1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the age of the universe in years.

List the known quantities:

- The Hubble constant, $H_{0}$ = 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- 1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s

Substitute the values into the age of the universe equation:

- Age of the universe = $\frac{1}{H_{0}}$
- Age of the universe = $\frac{1}{2.2\times10^{-18}}=4.54\times10^{17}s$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the age from seconds into years:

- Age of the universe = $\frac{4.54\times10^{17}}{3.15\times10^{7}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Age of the universe = $1.4\times10^{10}\mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The age of the universe will always come out as around 14 billion years (14 × 10*<sup>*9*</sup>* years), so if your answer in the exam is ever wildly off from this you know that something has gone wrong in your calculation (most likely some powers or putting numbers in your calculator incorrectly!). *

> *You can also remember this value from the intro theme tune to 'The Big Bang Theory' American sitcom:*

> *'**Our whole universe was in a hot, dense state** **Then nearly fourteen billion years ago expansion started, wait**'*

parts.problem_md:
Newton assumed that the universe was infinite, uniform and static. The Big Bang model suggests space and time originated at one point around 14 billion years ago. At this time the temperature was very high.

In 1965, Penzias and Wilson discovered cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation with a wavelength of around 1 mm.

Determine the current temperature of the CMB.

Surface temperature of the Sun = 5800 K

Peak wavelength emission of the Sun = 500 nm
parts.solution_md:
Determine the current temperature of the CMB:

List the known quantities:

- Surface temperature of the Sun, $T_{Sun}$ = 5800 K
- Peak wavelength emission of the Sun, $λ_{Sun}$ = 500 nm
- Peak wavelength emission of the CMB, $λ_{CMB}$ = 1 mm

Use Wien's law to determine the temperature of the CMB:

- Wien's law:  $T\propto\frac{1}{λ_{max}}$
- Therefore, $\frac{T_{CMB}}{T_{Sun}}=\frac{λ_{Sun}}{λ_{CMB}}\RightarrowT_{CMB}=T_{Sun}\times\frac{λ_{Sun}}{λ_{CMB}}$
- $T_{CMB}=5800\times\frac{500\times10^{-9}}{1\times10^{-3}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $T_{CMB}=2.9K$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

**Fig. 1.1**

This radiation was first emitted around 300 000 years after the Big Bang, during a stage of the universe's history called the 'era of recombination'.

At this stage, the radiation was in the visible region of the spectrum and had a temperature of around 3000 K.

Determine the factor by which the universe has expanded since the universe was at a temperature of 3000 K.
parts.solution_md:
Determine the factor by which the universe has expanded:

- List the known quantities:

  - Initial temperature, $T_{then}$ = 3000 K
  - Final temperature, $T_{now}$ = 2.9 K (from **(a)**)

Use the relationship between energy and temperature for a photon:

- Energy-temperature relation for photons:  $E\proptoT$
- $\frac{energyofphotonsat3K}{energyofphotonsat3000K}=\frac{kT_{now}}{kT_{then}}=\frac{2.9}{3000}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{energyofphotonsat3K}{energyofphotonsat3000K}=0.00097$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for photon energy

- Photon energy:  $E=\frac{hc}{λ}\Rightarrowλ\propto\frac{1}{E}$
- $\frac{λofphotonsat3K}{λofphotonsat3000K}=\frac{1}{0.00097}=1030$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember, redshift tells us the **factor of expansion** of the universe at different points in time/space, so in a question like this, you need to think about the relationships you know to try and get a ratio in terms of *$\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}$

> *Since the difference in wavelengths between these temperatures is so large, *$\Deltaλ\approxλofphotonsat3K$

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

In 1965, Penzias and Wilson discovered cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation with a wavelength of around 1 mm.
Fig. 1.1 shows the map of microwave background radiation from the COBE satellite. It shows the variation in the mean temperature of the CMB in different parts of the sky. Fig. 1.1. This radiation was first emitted around 300 000 years after the Big Bang, during a stage of the universe's history called the 'era of recombination'. At this stage, the radiation was in the visible region of the spectrum and had a temperature of around 3000 K.

Using Fig. 1.1, your answers to **(a)** and **(b)**, and your knowledge of redshift and cosmology

(i) Describe how the CMB provides evidence for the Hot Big Bang model of the universe.

[2]

(ii) State and explain what the COBE data in Fig. 1.1 suggests about the temperature variation in the early universe.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) The CMB provides evidence for the Hot Big Bang model of the universe because:

**EITHER**

- The wavelength of the CMB has been redshifted by an expanding and cooling universe; **[1 mark]**
- The shorter wavelength in the past indicates the temperature must have been very high at the beginning; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- The temperature of the CMB has cooled considerably from *t* = 300 000 to now and even more since the Big Bang; **[1 mark]**
- This cooling was caused by the expansion of the universe / the stretching of spacetime; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The COBE data suggests that:

- The wavelength / intensity of the CMB is (almost) the same in all directions **OR** there is very little temperature variation in the CMB (on the scale of µK); **[1 mark]**
- This indicates that there was very little temperature variation in the early universe too; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md: State what is meant by redshift.
parts.solution_md:
Redshift is:

- The apparent wavelength of light is observed to be greater than its known / measured value; **[1 mark]**
- (Due to) an object / star / galaxy moving away (from an observer) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md: Explain how cosmologists are able to determine that light from a distant star has undergone redshift.
parts.solution_md:
Cosmologists are able to determine that light from a distant star has undergone redshift by:

- Examining the (lines in the) spectrum (of light from the star); **[1 mark]**
- And comparing the lines with its known spectrum (of light measured on Earth); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
The Big Bang theory attempts to explain the origin of the Universe.

Describe the main ideas of the Big Bang theory.
parts.solution_md:
The main ideas of the Big Bang theory are:

- The Universe started with an explosion / Big Bang; **[1 mark]**
- All matter and energy was concentrated at a (single) point; **[1 mark]**
- The explosion caused the universe to expand** **from this (single) point; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problem_md: Explain why the redshift of galaxies is considered to be evidence for the Big Bang theory.
parts.solution_md:
The redshift of galaxies is considered to be evidence for the Big Bang theory because:

- If the Universe is expanding, then it must have been closer together in the past; **[1 mark]**
- The expansion of the Universe can be extrapolated back to its point of origin (known as the Big Bang); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *If the Universe is expanding at a measurable rate, then it makes sense that if we were able to rewind this expansion we would find a point in time where the Universe existed at a single point in time and space (called a singularity). This is the point at which the Big Bang is thought to have occurred. By doing this, scientists have been able to estimate the age of the Universe to be about 13.7 billion years old.*

parts.problem_md:
An astronomer analyses the light from a distant galaxy.

One of the observed spectral lines of hydrogen has a wavelength of 722 nm. The same spectral line has a wavelength of 656 nm when measured in the laboratory.

Calculate the factor by which the Universe has expanded since the light was emitted from the source.
parts.solution_md:
The Universe has expanded by:

- Factor = $\frac{722}{656}=1.1$ or 10% **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problem_md: Explain how comparing the values of cosmological redshift for distant galaxies provides evidence for the Big Bang theory.
parts.solution_md:
Comparing values of cosmological redshift for distant galaxies provides evidence for the Big Bang theory because:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- The more distant the galaxy, the longer the light travels through space and expands / stretches; **[1 mark]**
- The more distant the galaxy, the greater the redshift / expansion / stretching of wavelength; **[1 mark]**
- The more distant the galaxy, the faster it recedes / moves away (from an observer); **[1 mark]**

This provides evidence for the Big Bang theory because:

- (Increasing redshift suggests that) the universe is expanding; **[1 mark]**
- (Expansion suggests that) at an earlier point in time **OR** at the beginning / origin of time; **[1 mark]**
- The universe was a single point; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Cosmologists commonly quote the recessional velocity *v* of astronomical objects in relation to the speed of light *c*. This ratio is known as redshift *z*:

$z=\frac{v}{c}$

The Andromeda galaxy is the closest galaxy to our own Milky Way. Andromeda has a redshift value of z = −0.001.

State the significance of the minus sign and discuss its implication for the Milky Way and Andromeda in the distant future.
parts.solution_md:
The significance of the minus sign is:

- The light from Andromeda is <u>blue</u>shifted **OR** Andromeda is moving towards us / the Milky Way; **[1 mark]**

The implication of this is:

- Andromeda will hit / collide with the Milky Way (in the distant future); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Cosmologists commonly quote the recessional velocity v of astronomical objects in relation to the speed of light c. This ratio is known as redshift z: z = v/c

Table 1.1 contains information about two galaxies.

**Table 1.1**

| **Galaxy** | **Red-shift** | **Recessional velocity / km s**<sup>**−1**</sup> | **Distance / km** |
|---|---|---|---|
| NGC 247 | 8.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> |   | 1.1 × 10<sup>20</sup> |
| NGC 1357 |   | 1200 |   |

(i) Complete the missing information in Table 1.1.

[2]

(ii) Use the data to estimate the age, in years, of the Universe.

1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s

[4]
parts.solution_md:
List the known quantities:

- 1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) Complete Table 1.1:

| **Galaxy** | **Red-shift** | **Recessional velocity / km s**<sup>**−1**</sup> | **Distance / km** |
|---|---|---|---|
| NGC 247 | 8.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> | **Final answer:** **240** | 1.1 × 10<sup>20</sup> |
| NGC 1357 | **Final answer:** **4.0 × 10**<sup>**−3**</sup> | 1200 | **Final answer:** **5.5 × 10**<sup>**20**</sup> |

- Redshift:  $z=\frac{v}{c}\Rightarrowv=cz$
- Recessional velocity of NGC 247: * v* = (3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup>) × (8.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) = 240 000 = 240 km s<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**
- Redshift of NGC 1357:  $z=\frac{1200\times10^{3}}{3\times10^{8}}$ = 4.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> **[1 mark]**

Use Hubble's law to calculate the distance of NGC 247:

- Hubble's law:  $v=H_{0}d$ **[1 mark]**
- Distance of NGC 247:  $H_{0}=\frac{v_{247}}{d_{247}}=\frac{v_{1357}}{d_{1357}}\Rightarrowd_{1357}=d_{247}\times\frac{v_{1357}}{v_{247}}$
- Distance of NGC 247:  $d_{1357} = ( 1.1 \times 10^{20} ) \times \frac{1200}{240}$
- Distance of NGC 247:  $d_{1357}$ = 5.5 × 10<sup>20</sup> km **[1 mark]**

(ii) Estimate the age, in years, of the Universe:

- Hubble constant:  $H_{0}=\frac{v}{d}=\frac{240\times10^{3}}{1.1\times10^{20}}$
- Hubble constant: $H_{0}$ = 2.18 × 10<sup>−18</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**
- Age of Universe:  $t=\frac{1}{H_{0}}=\frac{1}{2.18\times10^{-18}}=4.58\times10^{17}s$
- Age of Universe:  $t=\frac{4.58\times10^{17}}{3.15\times10^{7}}=1.46\times10^{10}$ years **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 1.1 shows the emission spectrum of some wavelengths of light that were observed using a source in a laboratory.

![8-3-4c-e-hydrogen-spectrum-redshift-mcq-igcse](assets/002-8-3-4c-e-hydrogen-spectrum-redshift-mcq-igcse.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The same wavelengths of light were observed on an emission spectrum from a distant galaxy but were found to be redshifted.

Describe how you would expect the emission spectrum of the distant galaxy to look compared to the spectrum in Fig. 1.1.
parts.solution_md:
The redshifted emission spectrum would show:

- All the lines moved / shifted towards the 'long λ' side; **[1 mark]**
- By the same amount; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *When an object is moving away from an observer the wavelength of the light increases or becomes longer*

> *As the wavelength of light increases, it moves towards the red end of the spectrum, hence the name red shift*

> *Hence, all the lines will be shifted by the same amount *

![hydrogen-spectrum-redshift-mcq-igcse-ma](assets/003-hydrogen-spectrum-redshift-mcq-igcse-ma.png)

parts.problem_md:
An astronomer observes that light from a galaxy has been shifted towards the blue end of an emission spectrum.

State and explain what can be deduced about the motion of the galaxy from this observation.
parts.solution_md:
Blueshift means that:

- The galaxy is moving <u>towards</u> the observer; **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- Blueshift is a decrease in the observed wavelength of light (emitted from incoming stars and galaxies) **OR**
- The light from distant galaxies has a shorter wavelength than the same light observed on Earth; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The change in the wavelength of the observed light can tell us about the motion of the galaxy relative to the Earth*

- *If it is moving **away** from the Earth, the wave will spread out, hence the **wavelength will increase** and appear more **red** (hence the term 'red shift')*
- *If it is moving **towards **the Earth, the wave will bunch together, hence the **wavelength will decrease** and appear more** blue** (hence the term 'blue shift')*

parts.problem_md:
Hydrogen is an element of particular interest to cosmologists, as it can emit visible light waves.

A lot of useful information can be obtained by measuring the wavelength of the emitted light from the hydrogen in distant galaxies and comparing them to a laboratory sample. Some sample data is shown in Table 1.2.

**Table 1.2**

|   | **Wavelength in nm** |
|---|---|
| **Laboratory sample** | 486.14 |
| **Galaxy 1a** | 486.40 |
| **Galaxy 1b** | 484.85 |

Galaxy 1a and galaxy 1b are both moving relative to Earth.

Compare the motions of galaxy 1a and galaxy 1b relative to Earth.
parts.solution_md:
Compare the motions of galaxy 1a and galaxy 1b relative to Earth:

Determine the change in wavelength for galaxy 1a:

- $\Deltaλ=λ-λ_{0}$
- $\Deltaλ_{1a}$ = 486.40 − 486.14 = 0.26 nm
- (Therefore,) galaxy 1a is moving <u>away</u> from Earth; **[1 mark]**

Determine the change in wavelength for galaxy 1b:

- $\Deltaλ_{1b}$ = 484.85 − 486.14 = −1.29 nm
- (Therefore,) galaxy 1b is moving <u>towards</u> Earth; **[1 mark]**

State their relative speeds:

- (And) galaxy 1b is moving <u>faster</u> than galaxy 1a; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *If Δ**λ** is **positive** then the galaxy is **moving away** from the Earth. This is also known as **redshift**.*

> *If Δ**λ **is **negative** then the galaxy is **moving towards** the Earth. This is also known as **blueshift**.*

parts.problem_md:
The visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum from a star includes a dark line. This line is at a specific wavelength.

Fig 1.1 shows the position of the dark line in the spectrum from the Sun and in the spectrum from two different galaxies, galaxy A and galaxy B.

Explain what the spectrum ‘shifts’ of the dark lines tell us about the direction of the galaxies.
parts.solution_md:
The spectrum 'shifts' of the dark lines tell us that the galaxies are:

- Moving <u>away</u> from us / from Earth; **[1 mark]**
- Because the lines are shifted towards the <u>red</u> end of the spectrum / they have been redshifted; **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum from a star includes a dark line. This line is at a specific wavelength. Fig 1.1 shows the position of the dark line in the spectrum from the Sun and in the spectrum from two different galaxies, galaxy A and galaxy B.

Using Fig. 1.1, state which galaxy is

(i) moving faster,

[1]

(ii) closest to the Earth.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) The galaxy moving faster is:

- Galaxy B; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The galaxy that is closer to the Earth is:

- Galaxy A; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1a shows the variation of recession velocity v for a number of galaxies with their approximate distance d from Earth. Radiation from a star in a distant galaxy is analysed. Fig. 1.1b shows the spectral lines of the radiation from the star at different wavelengths compared to the same spectral lines produced by a source in the laboratory. Using the information in Fig. 1.1a and 1.1b, determine the distance of this galaxy from Earth.

From the mark scheme: λ_star = 480 nm AND λ_lab = 454 nm; Shift in wavelength Δλ = 480 − 454 = 26 nm; v = (3 × 10⁸) × (26/454) = 1.72 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹; Hubble constant H₀ = 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹; distance d = v/H₀ = 6.6 × 10²⁴ m.

Astronomers use the cosmic scale factor *R* to describe the scaling up of physical distances in the Universe.

As the universe expands, the wavelength of the detected radiation at a time *t* is larger than it was at a time* t*<sub>0</sub> in the past by a factor of

$\frac{R}{R_{0}}=1+z$

This expression represents the expansion rate of the universe.

Where* R* represents the separation of two galaxies at time *t*, *R*<sub>0</sub> represents the value of *R* at the time *t*<sub>0</sub> the radiation was emitted, and *z* represents the redshift, which is given by

$z\approx\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}\approx\frac{v}{c}$

(i) Using the scale factor, or otherwise, determine, in years, the approximate age of the universe at the instant when the detected light from the distant galaxy in** (a) **was emitted.

[4]

(ii) State the assumption that you made in your answer to **(b)(i)**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Determine the age of the universe when the light from the distant galaxy was emitted:

List the known quantities from **(a)**:

- Emitted wavelength, *λ* = 454 nm
- Change in wavelength, Δ*λ* = 26 nm
- Hubble constant, *H*<sub>0</sub> = 2.6 × 10<sup>−18</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the value of redshift for the galaxy:

- Redshift:  $z\approx\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}=\frac{26}{454}=0.057$ **[1 mark]**

Use the expression to determine the expansion rate of the universe:

- Expansion rate:  $\frac{R}{R_{0}}=1+z=1+0.057=1.057$
- Expansion rate:  $\frac{R}{R_{0}}=\frac{t}{t_{0}}=1.057$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the age of the universe:

- Age of the universe (now):  $t=\frac{1}{H_{0}}$
- $t=\frac{1}{2.6\times10^{-18}}=3.85\times10^{17}s$
- $t=\frac{3.85\times10^{17}}{60\times60\times24\times365}=12.2\times10^{9}\mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the age of the universe when the light was emitted:

- Age of the universe (then):  $\frac{t}{t_{0}}=1.057\Rightarrowt_{0}=\frac{t}{1.057}$
- $t_{0}=\frac{12.2\times10^{9}}{1.057}=11.5\times10^{9}\mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the universe was 11.5 billion years old when the light was emitted

(ii) The assumption made in the calculation is:

- The rate of expansion (of the universe) is uniform / constant / non-accelerated **OR** *H*<sub>0</sub> is constant over time; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The alternative method you could use is to consider how far the light has travelled in light years and subtract this from the age of the universe, this is because *

- *1 light year = the **distance** travelled by light in one year*
- *1 light year = speed of light (m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>*) × time (seconds in 1 year) *
- *1 light year = (3 × 10*<sup>*8*</sup>*) × (60 × 60 × 24 × 365)*

> *Although you are not required to know anything about light years for your exam, using your knowledge of light in this way can help to further your understanding of the topic of cosmology and the vast distances involved*

> *Over a distance of 6.6 × 10*<sup>*24*</sup>* m (from **(a)**), light has travelled*

- *distance (ly) = *$\frac{6.6 \times 10^{24} }{( 3 \times 10^{8} ) \times ( 60 \times 60 \times 24 \times 365 )}$* = 6.98 × 10*<sup>*8*</sup>* ly*

> *This means the light was emitted **0.7 billion years** ago*

> *At this time, the universe was (12.2 − 0.7) = **11.5 billion years old*

parts.solution_md:
(i) Determine Hubble's original estimate for the age of the universe:

List the known quantities:

Determine the gradient of the graph:

Compare to the modern estimate:

- Hubble's original estimate is about (12.2 − 1.9 =) 10 billion years lower than our modern estimate of the universe's age; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Measurements of the Hubble constant do not agree with each other because:

- Measurements from distant galaxies have large uncertainties;** [1 mark]**
- Galaxies that are close by (enough to observe finer detail) may have peculiar motion e.g. galaxies moving towards us (blueshifted) / (two or more) galaxies orbiting around a centre of mass etc; **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Two stars, A and B, in a binary system move in an anti-clockwise direction around a common centre of mass, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

Star A (inner orbit) is marked to the right of the centre of mass; Star B (outer orbit) is marked to the left of the centre of mass.

When measured in the laboratory, one of the spectral lines of hydrogen has a wavelength of 4.861 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m.

The same hydrogen line in the spectrum of one of the stars fluctuates from its laboratory wavelength by ± 0.420 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m and the line in the spectrum of the other star fluctuates by ± 0.865 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m.

Calculate the velocity of each star in the binary system and identify the faster star and the slower star.
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the velocity of the each star:

List the known quantities:

- Wavelength of spectral line in a lab, $λ$= 4.861 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m
- Change in wavelength of slower star, $\Deltaλ$= 0.420 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m
- Change in wavelength of faster star, $\Deltaλ$ = 0.865 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the velocity of the slower star:

- Doppler redshift:  $\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}\approx\frac{v}{c}\Rightarrowv=c\times\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}$
- Since $\Deltaλ\proptov$, for the slower star:  $\Deltaλ$ = 0.420 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m
- $v = ( 3.0 \times 10^{8} ) \times \frac{0.420}{4.861}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v=2.59\times10^{7}ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the velocity of the faster star:

- For the faster star:  $\Deltaλ$ = 0.865 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m
- $v = ( 3.0 \times 10^{8} ) \times \frac{0.865}{4.861}$
- $v=5.34\times10^{7}ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Identify the velocities of stars A and B:

- Orbital speed:  $v=\frac{2πr}{T}\Rightarrowv\proptor$
- Star A has the smaller orbital *r*, hence it is the slower star / $v_{A}=2.59\times10^{7}ms^{-1}$ **OR**
- Star B has the larger orbital *r*, hence it is the faster star / $v_{B}=5.34\times10^{7}ms^{-1}$; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

Determine the ratio of the orbits:

- Ratio:  $\frac{r_{B}}{r_{A}}=\frac{15.4\times10^{12}}{7.46\times10^{12}}=2.064=2.1$ **[1 mark]**
